title: REG U2·W4 — Business Law II: Agency, Secured Transactions, Bankruptcy & Entities (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — who is bound, who gets paid, which entity

Contracts answered whether a deal binds; this week answers three more business-law questions REG loves. Agency: when does an employee or manager bind MBG? Secured transactions: when MBG borrows against its equipment, who gets paid first? Bankruptcy: what happens when a debtor cannot pay? And the entity choice that determines the owner's personal exposure. These rules complete the REG business-law core.

Agency — the three kinds of authority

An agent binds a principal to the extent of the agent's authority. Actual express authority is what the principal explicitly grants; actual implied authority is what is reasonably necessary to carry out the express task; and apparent authority arises from the principal's manifestations to a third party that lead the third party reasonably to believe the agent is authorized — even if the agent secretly is not. A principal can also ratify an unauthorized act after the fact, adopting the whole transaction. Agents owe fiduciary duties of loyalty, obedience, and care; principals owe compensation and indemnification.

Principal liability in contract and tort

In contract, the principal is bound when the agent acted with authority (actual or apparent). In tort, respondeat superior makes a principal liable for an employee's torts committed within the scope of employment — but generally not for the torts of an independent contractor (a key distinction for a builder that uses many subcontractors). Whether the principal is disclosed, partially disclosed, or undisclosed affects whether the agent is also personally liable on the contract.

Secured transactions — attachment and perfection

UCC Article 9 governs security interests in personal property. A security interest attaches (becomes enforceable against the debtor) when three things coincide: value is given, the debtor has rights in the collateral, and there is an authenticated security agreement (or the creditor has possession/control). Perfection gives the creditor priority over third parties and is usually achieved by filing a financing statement; some collateral is perfected by possession or control, and a purchase-money security interest (PMSI) in consumer goods is perfected automatically. Perfection is the step that protects the lender against other creditors of MBG.

Priority and the PMSI superpriority

Among competing secured creditors, the general rule is first to file or perfect wins, and any perfected interest beats an unperfected one. The major exception is the PMSI superpriority: a properly perfected PMSI beats an earlier-filed general security interest in the same collateral. For equipment, the PMSI holder must perfect within 20 days of the debtor receiving the collateral; for inventory, the PMSI holder must file and give authenticated notice to existing secured parties before the debtor receives the inventory. A buyer in the ordinary course of business takes free of a security interest created by the seller.

Suretyship

A surety (or guarantor) promises to answer for another's debt — the bonding relationship from CMA's risk unit, here from the legal side. The surety who pays has rights of reimbursement from the principal debtor, subrogation to the creditor's position, exoneration (forcing the debtor to pay before the surety must), and contribution from co-sureties. The surety can assert the debtor's defenses on the underlying contract (but not the debtor's personal defenses such as incapacity), and is discharged to the extent the creditor releases collateral or materially modifies the obligation without consent.

Bankruptcy

Federal bankruptcy offers Chapter 7 (liquidation — a trustee sells nonexempt assets and distributes proceeds), Chapter 11 (reorganization — the business continues under a court-approved plan), and Chapter 13 (an individual's repayment plan from future income). Filing triggers an automatic stay that halts collection actions. Claims are paid by priority — secured creditors first from their collateral, then statutory priority unsecured claims (administrative expenses, certain wages, taxes), then general unsecured creditors. A trustee can recover preferential transfers (to a creditor within 90 days, or one year for insiders) and fraudulent transfers. Most debts are discharged, but some are nondischargeable — most taxes, debts from fraud, alimony/child support, and most student loans.

Choosing the entity and the liability shield

The entity decision trades off liability and tax. A sole proprietorship and a general partnership expose owners to unlimited personal liability; a limited partnership shields the limited partners (but not the general partner); an LLP and an LLC give all owners a liability shield with passthrough taxation; and a corporation shields shareholders but adds the C-corp double tax unless an S election is made. The shield is not absolute: a court may pierce the corporate (or LLC) veil when owners commingle funds, undercapitalize, ignore formalities, or use the entity to commit fraud. For MBG's owner, the LLC/S-corp combination from last week pairs the shield with passthrough taxation — the structure most contractors choose.

Federal securities and employment regulation

Two federal regimes round out business law. The Securities Act of 1933 regulates the initial issuance of securities, requiring registration and a prospectus unless an exemption applies — the most tested being the Regulation D private placements (limited offerings to accredited investors and a capped number of non-accredited investors). The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 regulates secondary trading and ongoing reporting by public companies, and its Rule 10b-5 is the broad antifraud provision that also reaches insider trading. Liability under §11 of the 1933 Act for a materially false registration statement can reach the issuer, its officers, and the CPA who certified the financial statements — a direct professional-liability exposure tying REG to the AUD material. On the employment side, an employer withholds and pays FICA (Social Security and Medicare) and pays FUTA unemployment tax on employees, but not on independent contractors — so worker classification is at once a tax question and the agency question from earlier in this lesson. Misclassifying employees as contractors to dodge payroll tax is a frequent enforcement target, with back taxes and penalties the cost of getting it wrong.

CMA bridge

CMA month 10 treated surety bonds and the certificate-of-insurance program as risk transfers; REG gives the legal mechanics — the surety's reimbursement and subrogation rights, the Article 9 priority that decides whether MBG's lender or a supplier is paid first, and the entity shield that protects the owner's personal assets behind the construction risk.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish actual, implied, and apparent authority; apply respondeat superior to employees (not independent contractors) within scope.
  2. Attach (value + debtor rights + security agreement) then perfect (usually by filing); know automatic PMSI-in-consumer-goods perfection.
  3. Apply priority — first to file or perfect, with the PMSI superpriority (20 days for equipment; file + notice before delivery for inventory).
  4. Know the bankruptcy chapters, the automatic stay, claim priority, preference recovery, and nondischargeable debts; match the entity to the liability/tax goal.

Recap: apparent authority flows from the principal's conduct toward third parties and respondeat superior reaches employees within scope; a security interest attaches with value, debtor rights, and an agreement, perfects (usually) by filing, and ranks first-to-file-or-perfect with a PMSI superpriority; bankruptcy's automatic stay and priority scheme order the payouts; and the LLC/S-corp shield protects the owner unless a court pierces the veil for commingling or undercapitalization; and federal securities law (the 1933 and 1934 Acts) and the employee-versus-contractor payroll rules round out the business-law core.

choices: The principal's manifestations to a third party
questions.explain: Apparent authority is created by the principal's conduct toward the third party, not by the agent alone.

questions.q: Under respondeat superior, a principal is liable for torts committed:
choices: By an employee within the scope of employment
By any agent in any circumstance
questions.explain: Respondeat superior reaches an employee's torts within the scope of employment, generally not an independent contractor's.

choices: Value is given, the debtor has rights in the collateral, and there is a security agreement
questions.explain: Attachment requires value, the debtor's rights in the collateral, and an authenticated security agreement (or possession).

questions.q: The general priority rule among perfected secured creditors is:
questions.explain: Among perfected creditors, priority generally goes to the first to file or perfect.

questions.q: A properly perfected purchase-money security interest (PMSI) generally:
choices: Has priority over earlier-filed security interests in the same collateral
Is always subordinate to earlier interests
questions.explain: The PMSI superpriority lets a properly perfected PMSI beat earlier-filed general security interests.

questions.q: Filing a bankruptcy petition triggers an:
choices: Auction of the debtor's exempt assets
End of the business in all cases
questions.explain: The automatic stay stops most collection efforts the moment the petition is filed.

questions.q: The limited liability of a corporation or LLC may be lost when a court:
choices: Pierces the veil for commingling, undercapitalization, or fraud
questions.explain: Courts pierce the veil when owners abuse the entity — commingling funds, undercapitalizing, or using it to commit fraud.
